海螺號,Conch (instrument),吹奏與氣息樂器,太平洋島嶼國家／南: Conch,Conch (instrument),Aerophones,Pacific island nations / South America / South Asia,instrument teaching,world instruments,instrument introduction
海螺號屬唇振氣鳴樂器，吹奏者以雙唇貼吹嘴送氣，靠自然圓錐管與口風控制泛音列發聲。: The conch is a lip-vibrated aerophone: the player presses the lips to the mouthpiece and blows, and the sound comes from the natural conical tube, with the embouchure choosing the overtones. Its timbre varies with the size and shape of the shell and with how fine or open the spiral is: a fine, sparse spiral gives a brighter sound, a coarser one a deeper sound. Most instruments have no fingerholes, and the pitch comes mainly from the player's embouchure and choice of overtone; the fundamental is not usually changed by holes.
海螺號常見於宗教與儀式場合：日本真言宗護摩儀式中與鼓同用，藏傳佛教法器亦見吹奏；: The conch is common in religious and ceremonial settings: in the Shingon goma ritual in Japan it is used together with the drum, and it is also blown as a Tibetan Buddhist ritual implement; in the Pacific islands it is used for welcome, funerals and summoning, and in Madagascar it appears at circumcision, funerals and royal ceremonies. Today it can be heard on the jazz player Steve Turre's Sanctified Shells and in film scores by the composers Jerry Goldsmith and Mychael Danna; Carlos Chávez's Xochipilli uses a trombone in place of the conch.
海螺號的發聲主體為大型海螺或法螺的貝殼，多取天然長成、顏色清白或帶花紋的右旋海螺: The sounding body of the conch is the shell of a large sea snail or triton, usually a naturally grown right-handed shell, plain white or patterned, about 25 to 33 cm long. The mouthpiece may be made of wood, bamboo, metal or the like and inserted into the end of the shell; the tip can also be ground through or drilled so that it is blown directly. Some instruments have holes drilled at both ends of the shell for a carrying cord, or are decorated with inlaid copper and silver plate; the more ornate ones have wing-shaped fittings of copper or silver, with rings at the tips and silk tassels and coloured ribbon tied on.
海螺號起源甚早，舊石器時代晚期馬格達倫期已有實例，巴勒斯坦約公元前第三千年紀亦見: The conch goes back a long way: there are examples from the Magdalenian period of the late Palaeolithic, and it was in use in Palestine around the third millennium BC as well. The Indian Atharvaveda records its religious use around 1000 BC, and it came to China with Buddhism and was kept up by the Tibetans, Mongols and other peoples; it also reached Japan in the Heian period and Korea, where it became a Buddhist ritual instrument. In Central America, the Caribbean, Oceania, Madagascar and in Wales and Malta in Europe it was used for worship, summoning, funerals and royal ceremony. After the twentieth century it entered jazz and film music too.
海螺號（法螺）是以大型海螺殼製成的唇振氣鳴吹奏樂器，H-S 分類編號 423.1: The conch (fa-luo) is a lip-vibrated aerophone made from a large sea-snail shell, H-S classification number 423.11. Its natural conical bore can sound with no change at all, or a blowhole can be opened at the end of the shell, or a mouthpiece of wood, bamboo or metal can be inserted; the player blows overtones with lip vibration, and fingerholes are very rarely added. It is found in the Pacific island nations, South America and South Asia, and is commonly used for religious ritual, summoning, welcome, funerals or military signals.
演奏海螺號時，可選未加工的海螺殼，或在螺端開吹口、裝入木、竹、金屬等材料製成的吹: To play the conch you can take an unworked shell, or open a blowhole at its tip and fit a mouthpiece made of wood, bamboo, metal or the like. Hold the opening of the shell, press the lips firmly against the mouthpiece and blow, using the embouchure to bring different pitches out of the overtone series; the size and shape of the shell affect pitch and timbre. A beginner first practises sealing the lips steadily on the mouthpiece and keeping the air going, then tries a single note and then a run of notes.
